bib.title: Statistical Power and Underpowered Statistics (Chapter 2)
bib.venue: Statistics Done Wrong (book chapter); publisher and year not printed in the extracted text

question: How much data is needed to detect an effect, and what goes wrong when studies are underpowered?
contributions: Explains statistical power through a coin-flip power curve
Shows consequences of underpowered studies: missed effects, truth inflation, extreme small-sample results
Recommends confidence intervals and assurance (AIPE) for sample sizing

results.claim: Flipping a coin 100 times, a true heads probability of 0.6 gives power 0.5 at p<0.05.
results.setup: Two-sided test of fair coin vs 60%-heads coin, 100 flips, alpha 0.05
results.quote:
I have a 50% chance of concluding that it’s rigged after
100 ﬂips.

results.claim: A fair coin gives 40 to 60 heads in 100 flips 95% of the time.
results.quote: I’ll get between 40 and 60 heads 95% of the time.

results.claim: With 1,000 flips a fair coin gives 469 to 531 heads 95% of the time, so power to detect 60% bias is near 1.
results.quote:
I’ll get between 469 and 531 95% of the
time.

results.claim: A heart attack trial cutting death risk from 20% to 10% needs 400 patients for 80% power.
results.quote:
you’d actually need
400 patients—200 in each control and treatment group.

results.claim: Scientists are usually satisfied with power of 0.8 or higher.
results.quote:
Scientists

are usually satisﬁed when the statistical power is 0.8 or higher

results.claim: Fewer than 3% of Science and Nature articles calculate power before the study.
results.quote:
fewer than 3% of articles
calculate statistical power before starting their study.

results.claim: More than four-fifths of negative RCTs in prestigious medical journals 1975-1990 lacked data to detect a 25% difference.
results.quote:
more than four-ﬁfths of randomized controlled trials
that reported negative results didn’t collect enough data to
detect a 25% difference

results.claim: Nearly two-thirds of those negative trials lacked power to detect a 50% difference.
results.quote:
nearly two-thirds of the negative trials
didn’t have the power to detect a 50% difference

the median
study has only a 20% chance of being able to detect the effect

results.claim: Cohen (1960) found average power 0.48 for medium effects in psychology journal studies.
results.setup: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology; medium = 0.5 SD
results.quote:
the average study had
only a power of 0.48 for detecting medium-sized effects

results.claim: Right-turn-on-red Virginia study: 308 accidents before and 337 after at 20 intersections was not significant, yet later studies found about 20% more collisions.
results.quote:
collisions were occurring roughly
20% more frequently

results.claim: Later studies found 60% more pedestrians run over in right-turn incidents.
results.quote:
60% more pedestrians were being run
over

results.claim: Kanazawa's corrected estimate: attractive parents 4.7% more likely to have girls, CI from 13.3% more to 3.9% less, with nearly 3,000 parents.
results.quote:
attractive parents were indeed 4.7% more likely
to have girls—but the conﬁdence interval stretched from 13.3%
more likely to 3.9% less likely.

results.claim: With a true 0.3% effect and 3,000 parents, significant results occur about 5% of the time and exaggerate the effect at least 20-fold; 40% of them point the wrong way.
results.quote:
40% of them will produce a wild overestimate
in favor of boys instead of girls.

results.claim: Illustrative power calculation by simulation: power is the fraction of simulated datasets with a significant result.
results.quote:
The power is simply the
fraction of datasets for which you obtain a statistically signiﬁcant
result.

limits: Chapter is a popular exposition; most figures are quoted from cited studies (endnotes not in the extract) and the book title, publisher and year are not printed in this PDF.
Author concedes assurance/AIPE methods exist for only some tests and are not widely adopted.
Shrinkage biases truly abnormal small counties toward the mean.
practices: Calculate power when designing a study to set sample size; consult Cohen's Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (Tips, p.28).
If the sample size is impractical, state the study's limitations (Tips).
Use assurance rather than power when you need to measure an effect to a given precision (Tips).
Treat 'statistically insignificant' as not meaning zero; report the estimate (Tips).
Be skeptical of results from clearly underpowered studies: truth inflation (Tips).
Report confidence intervals regardless of significance (Tips).
Compute confidence intervals when comparing groups of different sizes (Tips).
If power is hard to compute analytically, simulate many datasets with the expected effect and take the fraction significant (p.20).
Use shrinkage toward a global mean, or sort by the lower bound of a confidence interval, to rank items with unequal sample sizes (p.27-28).

terms.definition: The power of a study is the probability that it will distinguish an effect of a certain size from pure luck.
If a trial isn’t powerful enough to detect the effect it’s looking for, we say it is underpowered.
Also type M error or winner's curse: significant results from underpowered studies exaggerate the true effect size.
How often the confidence interval must beat our target width; used to choose sample size.
Accuracy in parameter estimation: sample size selection methods based on assurance.
Shrink estimates toward the overall average by a weighted average, weighting the average strongly when the group is small.
